item.title: ffmpeg-webCLI enables privacy-first video editing in the browser
item.description:
ffmpeg-webCLI enables privacy-first video editing in the browser

A new browser-based video editor, ffmpeg-webCLI, has been released as a reference implementation of the Web-CLI architecture. Unlike cloud-based tools such as CloudConvert, Kapwing, or Ezgif that require file uploads and expose user data to servers, ffmpeg-webCLI performs all processing locally within the browser using WebAssembly and ffmpeg.wasm. This approach ensures that video files never leave the user’s device.

🔍 Overview

The tool is designed to make privacy a verifiable technical property rather than a policy promise. It addresses the limitations of existing cloud services, which are subject to data breaches, subpoenas, and shifting privacy policies. By operating entirely client-side, ffmpeg-webCLI supports a wide range of video and audio manipulation tasks for free.

🧩 How it works

The underlying architecture is described in a paper defining four properties for sensitive data processing: fidelity, progressive disclosure, offline-first, and zero egress. The Web-CLI model argues that client-side processing should be the default for sensitive data. ffmpeg-webCLI implements this by running ffmpeg logic via WebAssembly directly in the user’s browser environment.

⚙️ Key details

ffmpeg-webCLI supports various operations, with a timeline slider allowing users to set start and end points for any task. Trimming is applied on top of other operations, enabling combined workflows such as extracting a clip, compressing it, and converting it to a GIF in a single pass.

  • GIF Creation: Converts video to animated GIFs with adjustable frame rate and output width. It uses a two-pass palette generation process to maintain color quality.
  • Compression: Reduces file size without altering resolution. Users can adjust quality via a CRF slider (18 for near-lossless to 51 for maximum compression) and select an encoding preset (ultrafast to veryslow) to balance speed and efficiency. A live size estimate updates as settings change.
  • Resizing: Changes output dimensions in a single pass. Width and height fields are auto-filled from the source, but users can edit them or leave them blank to let ffmpeg maintain the aspect ratio.
  • Audio Extraction: Strips the audio stream entirely, useful for creating silent loops or preparing clips for new audio.
  • Speed Adjustment: Alters playback speed between 0.25× and 4×. The system adjusts video PTS and the atempo audio filter chain to preserve pitch and sync, automatically chaining multiple atempo stages for multipliers outside the 0.5–2.0 range.
  • Frame Extraction: Pulls a single frame from any point in the video. Frames are initially extracted as PNG using ffmpeg, with JPEG output generated in-browser via a canvas.
  • Orientation and Cropping: Allows users to correct orientation, create mirror effects, or trim frames to specific regions. X/Y offsets and dimensions are auto-filled from source video properties.

💡 Why it matters

For users handling sensitive data, client-side processing eliminates the need to trust third-party servers with personal files. By keeping the data on the local device, the tool removes the risk of server-side leaks, legal subpoenas, or changes in corporate privacy policies. It provides a technical guarantee of data privacy that relies on architecture rather than corporate trust.

item.title: Forge Neo Remi introduces a Gradio-free, Anima-first Stable Diffusion workbench
item.description:
Forge Neo Remi introduces a Gradio-free, Anima-first Stable Diffusion workbench

Forge Neo Remi is a new downstream distribution of Forge Neo, built as an Anima-first Stable Diffusion WebUI workbench. It replaces the traditional Gradio interface with a fast, Gradio-free React 19 single-page application (SPA) powered by FastAPI, aiming to provide a zero-node, conflict-safe environment for studio-grade AI image creation on consumer hardware.

🔍 Overview

Remi is an independent downstream branch, not an official release of Forge Neo or any bundled model family. It pairs Forge Neo’s runtime and modern DiT model stack with a reimagined web workbench. The system is designed to be Anima-first and multi-DiT capable, utilizing a persistent job queue managed via SQLite and exposed through a REST API.

🧩 How it works

The core of Remi is its shift away from node-based graph wiring toward integrated, conflict-safe workflows.

  • Remi.UI Architecture: The interface uses declarative, capability-driven controls defined in remi.ui v1. It features refined light and dark themes, phone layouts, full keyboard control, and reload-free language switching between English and Simplified Chinese.
  • Model Capability Logic: The ModelCapability system automatically hides panels that do not apply to the loaded model family, providing clear reasons for exclusion. It displays quantization and capability badges (including Diffusers, GGUF, INT8-ConvRot, FP8, NVFP4, Turbo, RGBA, and Control) and offers actionable pre-submit workflow advice with one-click fixes.
  • Workflows: Users can execute Linear Multi-Stage Pipelines (Prompt Upsample → Generate → Refine → Finish) with content-addressed upstream stage caching. This allows downstream parameter changes to reuse earlier outputs without manual node wiring. Cross-model “Recipes” allow saving and applying conflict-checked parameter subsets.

⚙️ Key details

Remi is engineered to run on 8–24 GB consumer GPUs and Apple Silicon unified memory.

Component Description
UI Framework React 19 SPA with FastAPI backend; no Gradio dependency.
Inference Workers Supports in-process execution by default, or isolated inference via WorkerProtocol flags (--worker-process, --worker-gpus, --worker-mlx).
Model Support Full support for 2B, 2.9B, and 3.8B models (28/40/52-block layouts) with native Qwen3.5 semantic connector.
Apple Silicon Includes MPS dequantized-weight caching, unified-memory awareness, and optional MLX/mflux sidecar via --worker-mlx.

Note: While worker process flags are available, the queue currently does not dispatch to isolated workers and still runs every job in-process.

🎨 Features and Tools

  • Asset Management: Gallery Boards for organization, Asset Lineage for tracing parent/child outputs, and a pixel slider for comparing two runs via structured Parameter Diff.
  • Transparency: Lightbox allows switching between four backdrops to inspect alpha transparency.
  • Reference Integration: Send-to-Reference-Image function with model-aware slot badges (<image_1>, ref_image_0, ref_0).
  • Prompting: Multimodal/Local Prompt Upsampler (PUP) and a JSON Builder for composing structured layouts in MOSS-Image, FLUX.3 Layout, and Bria Fibo 2.0 VGL 2.0.
  • Control & LoRA: Supports cross-depth LoRA, ControlNet-LLLite remapping, Control-LoRA, VACE, and native samplers/guidance. “Anima Remi Presets” provide safe baselines with mutually exclusive stacks locked before sampling.
  • Testing & Diagnostics: Includes versioned remi.ui APIs, per-extension diagnostics (load times, errors), and a remi.testing contract verifier. Frequently used extensions are ported to remi.ui and guarded by automated Python, Vitest, and Playwright + axe gates.

🚀 Availability

Remi favors integrated workflows over compatibility with every legacy extension. Third-party extensions built for the old Gradio UI must be ported to remi.ui to function within this environment.

item.title: VS Code extension enables Python in Web via WebAssembly
item.description:
VS Code extension enables Python in Web via WebAssembly

A new VS Code extension allows users to run Python code in the Web, such as in vscode.dev, using WebAssembly as the execution engine. The project is designed primarily as an experimentation environment to help the VS Code team gain experience with running Python code in the Web using WebAssembly technologies.

🧩 How it works

The extension utilizes a pre-configured Python environment based on CPython WebAssembly builds, specifically the Python-3.11.0rc1-wasm32-wasi-16.zip build. It depends on the GitHub Repositories extension and requires users to authenticate with GitHub.

Users can set up their own Python environment, including source wheel Python packages, by following these steps:

  • Create a new GitHub repository.
  • Download a wasm-wasi-16 build from the tiran/cpython-wasm-test releases and expand it into the root of the repository.
  • To add source wheel packages, create a site-packages folder in the root.
  • Install the package using the command pip install my_package --target ./site-packages (requires a local Python installation with pip).
  • Commit the changes.
  • Change the python.wasm.runtime setting to point to the user’s GitHub repository.

⚙️ Key details

The extension is not intended for productive Python development due to several limitations:

  • No pip support.
  • No socket support.
  • No support for native Python modules.
  • No thread support.
  • No async support, as a consequence of the lack of thread support.

Regarding versioning, odd major, minor, or patch version numbers indicate an insider or pre-release. For example, 1.0.0 and 0.1.0 are pre-releases, while 2.0.2 is a regular release. The initial version was 0.5.0, and version 0.7.0 added basic debugging support.

💡 Why it matters

This project serves as a testbed for integrating WebAssembly with Python in web-based development environments. It also outlines contribution requirements, noting that most contributions require agreeing to a Contributor License Agreement (CLA) to grant rights to use the contribution.

item.title: ИИкона 1.9.7: AI integration for 1C supporting multiple model providers
item.description:
ИИкона 1.9.7: AI integration for 1C supporting multiple model providers

ИИкона, an extension for working with language models directly within 1C, has released version 1.9.7. This update provides a common connector that enables features such as expert chats, database access tools, knowledge search, AI-annotated error monitoring, and diagram generation. The release has been verified on 1C:Enterprise 8.3.27.1989 and BSP 3.1.11.466.

🧩 How it works

The extension operates through a unified connector that interfaces with various AI models. Availability of tools and attachments depends on the specific model and its API.

  • Model Support: Supports OpenAI-compatible APIs, Anthropic, Google Gemini, YandexGPT, and GigaChat.
  • Additional Providers: Via compatible APIs, users can connect to OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Mistral, and Qwen. Local models can be accessed through Ollama and LM Studio.
  • Subscriptions: A separate adapter is provided for personal subscription-based connections.

⚙️ Key details

  • Vector Search: Qdrant is connected for vector search capabilities.
  • Diagram Rendering: Kroki and Mermaid are used for rendering diagrams.
  • Name Recognition: A specific service is connected for name recognition tasks.
  • Security: API keys are stored in the protected storage of BSP (БСП).
  • Developer Access: Developers can invoke the common connector from their own code.

🚀 Availability and Setup

The release is distributed as a .cfe file. Installation involves connecting the file via “Administration → Configuration Extensions” and updating the database. Users configure pre-set models in “AIkonna → Administration → AI Models” and verify connections in the model cards. After setting up an expert with a system prompt, users can interact via the “Expert Chat” interface, using Ctrl+Enter to send messages and attaching files via the button next to the question input.

💡 Why it matters

Version 1.9.7 passed 1,178 primary tests via EDT, 105 role-based executions, and compilation checks. The Sonar Quality Gate status is OK with zero open remarks. The release acknowledges Sergey Boyko for regular testing on “Trade Management,” detailed logs, reproducible scenarios, and suggestions regarding multi-database work, metadata retrieval, agent loop limits, and cost estimation.

agent_learning: An Open-Source AI Agent Development Textbook

An open-source AI Agent textbook and learning repository called agent_learning has been released to address the skill gap between calling an LLM API and building a complete Agent system. The resource provides a systematic tutorial covering the full lifecycle of agent development, from foundational concepts to production deployment.

🧩 How it works

The textbook is structured to guide developers through the core components of agentic systems. It covers the transition from basic capabilities to advanced deployment strategies, including:

  • Core Capabilities: Function calling, memory systems, planning, RAG, and context engineering.
  • Advanced Topics: Agentic RL, multi-agent systems, and self-evolving agents.
  • Production Readiness: Evaluation, security, and deployment pipelines.

The curriculum includes 26 chapters organized across six main areas: foundations, core capabilities, frameworks, multi-agent systems, production, and capstone projects. The material bridges theoretical papers and practical application by providing explanations for techniques such as ReAct, Reflexion, MemGPT/Letta, GraphRAG, and GRPO.

item.title: Agent-based trading simulation using Google ADK and A2A protocol
item.description:
Agent-based trading simulation using Google ADK and A2A protocol

This project demonstrates an agent-based trading system simulation featuring distinct agents for trading logic and risk management, communicating via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. It includes a web-based simulator UI to configure, run, and visualize trading strategy performance.

🔍 Overview

The system consists of three main services interacting via HTTP and the A2A protocol. It leverages the open A2A protocol for standardized, interoperable communication between the agents. This allows agents built with different frameworks to discover capabilities and interact securely. The entire system is built using the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK).

🧩 How it works

The workflow begins with the Simulator UI taking simulation parameters from the user. It then runs the market simulation loop. For each step, the Simulator calls the AlphaBot service via A2A tasks/send, providing current market data and portfolio state. AlphaBot analyzes the data to determine a potential trade signal. If a trade is proposed, AlphaBot calls the RiskGuard service with the trade proposal and portfolio state. RiskGuard evaluates the proposal against configured rules and returns an approval or rejection. The final trade decision is returned to the Simulator, which updates the portfolio state based on executed trades.

⚙️ Key details

  • AlphaBot: Implements a Simple Moving Average (SMA) crossover strategy to propose trades. It calculates SMAs to determine BUY or SELL signals and updates its internal state.
  • RiskGuard: Evaluates trade proposals against configurable risk rules, including max position size and max portfolio concentration.
  • Simulator UI: A FastAPI-based web application that allows users to configure parameters for market conditions (initial price, volatility, trend), trading strategy (SMA periods, trade quantity), and risk rules. It visualizes results using Plotly, displaying price action, SMA indicators, portfolio value, and trade execution markers on interactive charts.
  • Deployment: Includes scripts for easy local execution and deployment to Google Cloud Run. Dockerfiles are provided for building container images for each service, facilitated by Google Cloud Build.

💡 Why it matters

The project demonstrates how distinct AI agents can collaborate in a specific domain (trading) using the A2A protocol. By separating trading logic from risk management into different agents that communicate securely and interoperably, the system showcases a modular approach to building multi-agent applications where each agent focuses on a specialized task.

item.title: Automated AI paper writing skill pack for coding agents released
item.description:
Automated AI paper writing skill pack for coding agents released

A new open-source skill pack has been released that enables standard coding agents to execute the multi-agent pipeline defined in the PaperOrchestra framework, turning unstructured research materials into submission-ready LaTeX papers. The tool operates without requiring API keys or LLM SDK dependencies, delegating all language model reasoning and web search capabilities to the host agent’s native tools.

🔍 Overview

The project transforms the specific prompts, schemas, halt rules, and verification pipelines from the PaperOrchestra paper into host-agent-executable skills. It supports a wide range of coding agents, including Claude Code, Cursor, Antigravity, Cline, Aider, OpenCode, and OpenClaw. The underlying PaperOrchestra framework, defined by Song, Y., Song, Y., Pfister, T., and Yoon, J., utilizes a five-agent pipeline that outperforms single-agent and tree-search baselines on the PaperWritingBench benchmark, showing absolute win margins of 50–68% on literature review quality and 14–38% on overall quality.

🧩 How it works

The system consists of a top-level driver skill and several specialized sub-skills that coordinate the paper writing process. The pipeline allows Steps 2 and 3 to run in parallel.

  • paper-orchestra: The top-level driver that coordinates the other six skills.
  • outline-agent: Step 1. Converts idea, log, template, and guidelines into a structured outline JSON containing plotting, literature review, and section plans.
  • plotting-agent: Step 2. Executes the plotting plan, renders plots and conceptual diagrams, and captions them.
  • literature-review-agent: Step 3. Conducts web searches, verifies candidates via Semantic Scholar, and drafts the Introduction and Related Work sections with high citation integration.
  • section-writing-agent: Step 4. Drafts remaining sections in a single multimodal call, builds tables from experimental logs, and splices figures.
  • content-refinement-agent: Step 5. Runs simulated peer review and applies strict halt rules to accept or revert changes.
  • paper-writing-bench: Reverse-engineers raw materials from existing papers to build benchmark cases.
  • paper-autoraters: Executes the paper’s own automated raters for citation F1, literature review quality, and side-by-side paper quality.
  • claim-evidence-audit: An optional post-pipeline skill that maps claims to log numbers, figures, or verified citations and enforces coverage thresholds.

⚙️ Key details

Each skill is composed of three distinct components that ensure deterministic behavior where possible:

  • SKILL.md: A dense instruction document the host agent reads and follows.
  • references/: Contains verbatim paper prompts, JSON schemas, rubrics, halt rules, and example outputs.
  • scripts/: Purely deterministic local helpers for JSON schema validation, Levenshtein fuzzy matching, BibTeX formatting, deduplication, LaTeX sanity checks, and coverage gates.

There are no network calls, LLM calls, or API keys embedded within the skill scripts. An optional pre-pipeline skill aggregates scattered coding-agent history into the structured idea.md and experimental_log.md inputs required by PaperOrchestra. If these inputs already exist, this aggregation step is skipped, and the main pipeline proceeds directly. Users can trigger this by pointing their agent at a directory containing research notes.

🚀 Availability

The skill pack is designed for developers and researchers using coding agents who need to automate the transition from experimental logs to formal academic papers. It requires no special environment setup beyond the host coding agent’s capabilities, as it relies on the agent’s native tools for LLM reasoning and web search.

item.title: OpenQodex adds pre-push code review for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor
item.description:
OpenQodex adds pre-push code review for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor

Open source code review tool OpenQodex now runs inside coding agents to check every change before you push. It operates without requiring a separate account or API key, acting as a separate reviewer that validates code changes made by agents in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Cline.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenQodex is an open source code review tool for coding agents.
  • It runs a separate reviewer that checks every change an agent writes before the user pushes.
  • No account or key of its own is required.
  • It is available for use in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Cline.

🧩 How it works

  • Code Graph: A code graph provides the agent with a map of the codebase.
  • Scanner Integration: It runs scanners that fit the changed files, keeping findings on the changed lines. A scanner is a program that checks code without a model, such as gitleaks or semgrep.
  • Dependency Check: Every supported lockfile in the repository is checked against osv.dev at every review and scan of a change. Advisories outside the changed lines are shown but never counted.
  • Fresh Reviewers: Separate Claude Code or Codex processes on the user’s login run the review, with no memory of the current session.
  • Verification: A script checks every line a reviewer quotes as evidence against the code. Verifiers confirm or refute every candidate and every scanner finding.

⚙️ Key details

  • Initiation: Users say to their agent, “review my change with openqodex”.
  • Setup: The init command finds agents on the machine, lists the files it will write, and asks for confirmation once.
  • Terminal Execution: In your own terminal, run ~/.openqodex/bin/openqodex review.
  • Sandbox Limitation: In its default sandbox, Codex gives commands no network, so the terminal command must be run outside the sandbox.
  • Scope: The review covers commits not yet pushed plus everything uncommitted.
  • Output: The tool prints a receipt with the verdict, one line per finding, and the path to report.html. It also writes report.md, report.json, and report.sarif.

🚀 Availability

  • Works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Cline, and Goose.
  • The host identifier can be claude-code, codex, cursor, cline, or goose.
  • An npx install does not put OpenQodex on the system PATH.

item.title: Octocode: A Rust CLI and MCP server for codebase intelligence
item.description:
Octocode: A Rust CLI and MCP server for codebase intelligence

Octocode is a Rust CLI and MCP server designed for exploring codebases by combining semantic search, structural search, and a live graph of symbols and dependencies. It provides AI agents, such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Windsurf, with deep understanding of code structures through a single binary.

🧩 How it works

The tool integrates several capabilities to assist with code exploration:

  • Find code by intent: Uses hybrid vector and keyword search with configurable reranking.
  • Locate definitions and usages: Performs structural search over the current source.
  • Trace relationships: Maps imports, calls, inheritance, and implementations between files and symbols.
  • Read signatures: Accesses function signatures without loading entire files, optionally using a language server for definitions, references, and hover information.
  • Run locally: Utilizes default embedding and reranking models or configurable remote providers.

⚙️ Key details

Octocode operates through specific tools that differ in their indexing requirements:

Tool Use it for Requires an index
semantic_search Find code, documentation, and indexed history by meaning Yes
structural_search Find definitions, usages, and AST patterns in current source No
view_signatures Read function signatures, declarations, and imports No
graphrag Explore live file and symbol relationships and dependency paths No
lsp_* Definitions, references, hover information, symbols, and completion No; requires a language server

Structural search, signatures, and the live dependency graph read the current source directly and function without an index. In contrast, semantic search relies on an index created by running commands in the project’s Git repository. The default configuration uses local FastEmbed models, which download on first use without requiring an API key. For directories without Git, users can apply octocode index --no-git.

🚀 Availability

Installation methods include:

  • Using an installer on Linux or macOS, or in a Unix-compatible shell on Windows.
  • Downloading a binary from GitHub Releases or installing the published crate.
  • Building from source, which requires Rust 1.95 or later and protoc.

Users can integrate Octocode with various MCP clients by installing it where the client can find it on the PATH and adding an entry to the client’s MCP configuration. Additionally, the companion AI agent runtime, Octomind, includes Octocode and OctoFS capabilities in its developer:general agent. The first run of Octomind may install required tools and ask for model credentials.

item.title: Sandbox API now scales to 50,000 microVMs in 10-15 seconds
item.description:
Sandbox API now scales to 50,000 microVMs in 10-15 seconds

The Sandbox API now supports a high-performance serving path that scales to 50,000 running microVMs in 10–15 seconds by scatter-gathering per-node inventory instead of storing per-sandbox objects.

🔍 Overview

The system introduces three distinct serving paths for the Sandbox API:

  • Pod path: An upstream controller translates a Sandbox into a standard Pod.
  • L3 path: A custom sandbox-apiserver serves the sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1 API directly from NodeInventory.
  • e2b path: An optional REST surface compatible with the e2b SDK, accessible via Kubernetes or an external mesh.

🧩 How it works

The L3 path utilizes a scatter-gather methodology for node inventory. Rather than creating a Kubernetes object for every single sandbox, the system claims sandboxes from a node’s warm pool during creation. This approach significantly reduces load on the control plane; in a specific test environment, patching a SandboxWarmPool took 20 bare-metal nodes to 50,000 running microVMs in 10–15 seconds, with etcd seeing approximately 2 writes per second.

Serving Paths Details

  • Pod path: Routing Pods to microVM nodes is handled via an explicit pod-template contract written by the template author.
  • L3 path: The sandbox-apiserver adds subresources for pause, resume, fork, and snapshot operations.
  • e2b path: The sandbox-envd-proxy carries SDK traffic for files, commands, and PTY into the sandbox. Outside of Kubernetes, sandbox-e2b can serve the same interface on a sandboxd mesh using gossip-based node discovery.

⚙️ Key details

The deployment chart includes a warm-pool driver and an APIService that shadows the Sandbox CRD for agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1. This design ensures that an L3 cluster does not run the upstream controller or install its Sandbox CRD. Users selecting the Pod path must instead apply the upstream sandbox-with-extensions.yaml.

Component Function
sandbox-apiserver Serves the L3 API and e2b REST surface from NodeInventory
sandbox-envd-proxy Carries e2b SDK data plane traffic into the sandbox
sandbox-e2b Serves e2b surface on a sandboxd mesh outside Kubernetes
sandboxd Node-local daemon used by the L3 apiserver and proxy

💡 Why it matters

By decoupling the high-frequency sandbox lifecycle operations from etcd storage, this architecture enables rapid scaling of microVMs. It also provides flexibility for developers to use either standard Kubernetes Pod abstractions or a specialized L3 API for lower-latency sandbox management, while maintaining compatibility with the e2b developer experience.

ToolHive: An enterprise platform for managing Model Context Protocol servers

ToolHive is an enterprise-grade platform designed for running and managing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. It allows organizations to run any MCP server securely, instantly, and anywhere, addressing the need for secure and observable MCP infrastructure in production environments.

🔍 Overview

ToolHive addresses the challenges of managing MCP servers by providing a modular architecture that streamlines secure server management and integration. Unlike most MCP solutions that are SaaS-based, ToolHive allows companies to self-host their MCP registry and gateway, which is particularly useful when compliance requirements prohibit sensitive information from being processed by SaaS providers. The platform includes a Kubernetes operator, enabling teams to declare policies and integrate with identity and observability stacks using familiar tools and patterns.

🧩 How it works

At its core, ToolHive wraps every MCP server in an isolated container with a minimal permission file that does not include local credentials. This isolation helps enforce security standards. The platform uses semantic tool search to reduce token usage by up to 85%. When configured with an authentication source, ToolHive enforces identity and access policy per request, giving platform teams the observability required for production environments. It also provides audit logs and configurable identity enforcement to address security concerns regarding shadow MCP use by developers.

⚙️ Key details

The platform offers a range of features for managing MCP infrastructure, including:

  • Defining dedicated endpoints for secure and efficient team access to tools
  • Orchestrating multiple tools into a virtual MCP using a deterministic workflow engine
  • Centralizing control of security policy, authentication, authorization, and auditing
  • Integrating with Identity Providers (IdP) for Single Sign-On (SSO) via OIDC/OAuth compatibility
  • Customizing and filtering tools and descriptions to improve performance and reduce token usage
  • Connecting with local clients such as Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and VS Code Server
  • Curating a catalog of trusted servers for quick discovery and deployment
  • Integrating with the official MCP registry and adding custom MCP servers
  • Grouping servers based on role or use case
  • Managing the registry via an API-driven interface or embedding it in existing workflows
  • Verifying provenance and signing servers with built-in security controls
  • Providing preset configurations and permissions for a frictionless user experience

item.title: MiniMax H3 Director: New ComfyUI Node for Multi-Clip Video Generation
item.description:
MiniMax H3 Director: New ComfyUI Node for Multi-Clip Video Generation

MiniMax H3 Director is a new ComfyUI node designed for long video and multi-segment generation. It integrates segment planning, conditional encoding, sampling, decoding, and export into a single interface, utilizing the official MiniMax H3 Image-to-Video and Reference-to-Video models alongside KSampler and AV separation decoding pipelines. The node natively outputs stereo audio.

🧩 How it works

The node manages a visual timeline for video generation, supporting several task types and advanced control over segmentation and transitions.

  • Segmentation and Editing: Users can upload video within the node to split, equally divide, or intelligently segment scenes using PySceneDetect. Split points are selectable and deletable, with a visual timeline previewing each segment’s range and thumbnail.
  • Grouped Keyframes: An independent first-last frame timeline allows multiple keyframe groups. Users can either write prompts for text-to-video or upload first/last frames (officially supporting last-frame-only uploads).
  • Inter-Segment Guidance: When enabled, empty groups use the last N frames of the previous segment for motion and audio continuity. Users can adjust duration via dragging and select specific groups to run.
  • Prompt Syntax: Prompts utilize <Picture N>, <Video K>, or <Audio J> tags (or @ references). The timeline preview and selection states remain synchronized with the prompts.
  • Reference Binding: For style-source video timelines, each segment’s source frame is automatically bound to <Video 1>. For reference-to-video tasks, additional reference images (up to 9) and audio (up to 3) can be attached per group.
  • Selective Sampling: When enabled, only checked segments or material groups are sampled. Unchecked segments can be filled with cache or source frames during export.
  • Audio Integration: Audio is generated in the same sampling pass as the visuals. For video-to-video and reference-video tasks, users can choose to generate sound, use original audio, or remain silent.
  • Reference Audio Slots: Users can select existing videos or local audio/video files. Selected videos immediately extract the first audio track as FLAC, saved directly to the input/ directory.

⚙️ Key details

The node supports various task types and integrates external modules to refine the generation pipeline. A semantic bridge and self-lift module can be attached to specific ports; if unconnected, the system behaves as a standard single-stage one-sampling process. When connected, the self-lift module transforms the process into a low-resolution prefix, 3D lift, and high-resolution finish, using Euler sampling at the director canvas resolution.

External Modules and Refinement

Module/Feature Functionality
Semantic Bridge Uses a student MLP to rewrite official conditional tokens. Weights are not distributed with the plugin and must be placed in models/semantic_bridge/.
Self-Lift Connects to the selflift port. Enables a multi-stage sampling process (low-res prefix + 3D lift + high-res finish).
Refine Connects to the refine port. Offers three modes: refine (same-resolution refinement), upscale (upscale to target canvas then re-sample according to SIGMAS), and latent_upscale (upscale H3 latent only, no re-sampling).
Report Output Outputs the segment plan and per-segment task summary via the report port.

Model and Configuration Requirements

  • CLIP Loader: The type must be set to minimax (Qwen3-VL).
  • UNET Selection: t2v, i2v, and fl2v tasks use the fl2va UNET. r2v, v2v, and rv2v tasks use the ref2va UNET.
  • Distillation: The model is distilled from FL2VA. Note that r2v, v2v, and rv2v are forced compatibility modes, and caution is advised when using them.
  • ComfyUI Version: Users must upgrade ComfyUI to version 0.30.0 or higher.
  • Source Images: Outputting the original film to source_images fills the independent source_images output without altering the main images output.

🚀 Availability

The complete resource package, including MiniMax H3 model weights and example JSON workflows, is available via Comfyit Stirring Station · Article 506: “MiniMax H3 Models and Workflows.” After downloading, users must merge the models/ directory into ComfyUI/models/. The JSON workflow can be dragged directly into ComfyUI to begin use. The toolbar also supports importing and exporting director packages, which save timeline JSON and reference materials in a zip file.

item.description:
OpenTelemetry plugin enables comprehensive tracing and metrics for Hermes Agent

An OpenTelemetry plugin has been released for Hermes Agent, enabling detailed observability for AI agent workflows. This update allows every interaction and process within the agent to be tracked and exported to compatible backends.

🔍 Overview

The plugin integrates Hermes Agent with OpenTelemetry (OTel) standards. It captures various operational aspects of the agent, including:

  • Model calls and API requests
  • Tool calls and skill loads
  • Approvals and delegated sub-agents

All of these events are structured into a single OTel trace for each Hermes turn. This trace includes metrics for tokens, costs, and latency. Optionally, logs and structured events are also captured and exported to any OTLP backend via HTTP or gRPC.

🧩 How it works

The plugin uses a comprehensive attribute schema to log details across different components of the agent. Attributes are emitted in two conventions to support various backends:

  • OpenInference (llm.*, input.value): Optimized for Phoenix.
  • OTel GenAI (gen_ai.*): Optimized for Langfuse, Weave, and generic dashboards.

This dual-convention approach eliminates the need for custom mapping in backend configurations.

⚙️ Key details

Specific trace data includes:

Component Tracked Details
Skills Name, source (skill_view / path read), path; remains open until the turn ends
Model Calls Model, provider, input user message, output assistant response
Metrics Token counts (incl. cache and reasoning buckets), duration, finish reason, request parameters
Errors ERROR status, exception details, and retry metadata
Tool Calls Arguments, results, inferred target/command, and hermes.tool.outcome (completed, error, timeout, blocked, cancelled)
Approvals Decision wait time, choice (once, session, always, deny, timeout, smart_approve, smart_deny, smart_escalate), and who decided
Sub-agents Role, goal, status, duration, summary, child’s model, and total subtree cost
Kanban A card’s run is traced from the dispatcher’s claim through the worker’s turn

The hermes.query_source attribute distinguishes the origin of calls:

  • main: The agent loop’s own calls
  • subagent: A delegated child’s calls
  • auxiliary: Calls made on the agent’s behalf (e.g., titling, compression, Mixture-of-Agents references, vision). These are tagged with hermes.auxiliary.task.

For successful git commit operations, the plugin records hermes.tool.git_commit, which is also counted as a hermes.commit.count and a commit event.

🚀 Multi-agent Support

The plugin supports complex orchestration patterns:

  • Delegated children
  • Kanban workers operating on different profiles and models
  • Swarms
  • Mixture-of-Agents
  • Cron jobs

In multi-agent runs, child executions are nested within the trace, ensuring that a single connected trace represents the entire workflow. GPU and CPU utilization are monitored using host metrics.

🧩 How It Works

The tool is built on PowerShell, which serves as the cross-platform runtime. When executed, it writes configuration files native to the operating system:

  • Windows: Registry policies
  • macOS: Defaults or plist payloads
  • Linux: JSON policy files

The script starts in preview mode, meaning no changes are made until the user explicitly adds the -Apply flag. Before an apply run, the tool writes a backup unless the user specifies -NoBackup for policy-only changes. This backup can be restored using the -UndoFromBackup command.

Feature Area Example Commands/Policy Names

News BraveNewsDisabled
Talk BraveTalkDisabled
Playlist BravePlaylistEnabled

🚀 Usage

To use BraveDebloater, users pick features and copy the matching command from bravedebloater.tersa.tech. Each command previews first. To write the policy, the user adds -Apply and then restarts Brave. To undo changes, users follow the preview and apply commands provided in the Restore section.

item.title: Dunetrace introduces deterministic runtime monitoring for AI agents
item.description:
Dunetrace introduces deterministic runtime monitoring for AI agents

Dunetrace has introduced a runtime reliability layer designed specifically for AI agents. The tool addresses the issue of silent failures in agent systems, where APIs may return status code 200 and latency metrics appear normal, yet the underlying logic is broken. Unlike traditional tracers that answer “what happened?” after a failure is already known, Dunetrace answers “is something breaking right now?” using deterministic checks in the request path.

🧩 How it works

Dunetrace operates on the runtime path of AI agents, enabling it to block actions before they execute. It provides the following core capabilities:

  • Structural and semantic detection: Identifying issues through code structure and meaning.
  • Runtime prevention: Stopping problematic actions before they complete.
  • Native root cause identification: Determining the origin of failures.
  • One-click fixes: Providing immediate resolutions for detected issues.

The system uses zero-LLM checks on every run, meaning it does not rely on language model calls for its monitoring logic. This ensures deterministic behavior. The tool tracks LLM calls, including streaming, and outbound HTTP calls without requiring changes at the call site.

⚙️ Key details

Dunetrace distinguishes between “exact runs” and “implicit runs” based on how the agent is integrated:

  • Exact runs: Supported out-of-the-box for FastAPI, Flask requests, LangGraph invoke, CrewAI kickoff, and Vercel AI SDK wrappers.
  • Implicit runs: If specific entry points are not wrapped, Dunetrace records LLM calls as implicit runs. However, these runs remain in “shadow” mode, meaning their signals are held but no alerts are generated because the boundaries of the run are guessed.

The primary data structure consists of Sessions & Events, which log every run, tool call, and LLM exchange. This raw data serves as the foundation for all other monitoring features.

🚀 Availability and Setup

Dunetrace is available for local development and deployment with the following requirements:

  • System Requirements: Docker, plus either Python 3.11+ or Node.js 22+.
  • Local Startup: The service runs on localhost with authentication disabled by default. The curl -s localhost:8001/ready command should return {"status":"ok"}.
  • Integration: Users can start Dunetrace, observe it catching failures without API keys or LLM calls, and then add it to their own agent code.
  • Remote Setup: If the SDK runs on a different machine or container, users must set the DUNETRACE_ENDPOINT environment variable to the ingest URL.

💡 Why it matters

The primary value proposition of Dunetrace is shifting failure detection from post-mortem analysis to real-time prevention. By operating in the request path, it allows policies to block actions before execution, addressing the problem of silent failures that standard observability tools often miss because they only record what has already happened.

item.title: esptool-js brings browser-based serial flashing to Espressif chips
item.description:
esptool-js brings browser-based serial flashing to Espressif chips

esptool-js is a new Javascript implementation of esptool, a serial flasher utility for Espressif chips, that runs directly in supported web browsers using the Web Serial API.

🔍 Overview

The repository provides a tool for flashing firmware to ESP devices without requiring a local Python environment. It is designed to work with Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge version 89 or later, as well as Google Chrome on Android version 61 or later via the web-serial-polyfill compatibility layer.

🧩 How it works

The library operates through the following workflow:

  • Request access to a serial port using the Web Serial API, optionally filtering by USB vendor or product IDs.
  • Configure loader options and create an ESPLoader instance.
  • Connect to the ESP device and detect the chip, a process that resets the device.
  • Flash firmware images to the device.

Users can read firmware files from a File input or fetch request. Key configuration parameters include the starting address in flash, flash mode (e.g., “dio”), flash frequency (e.g., “40m”), and flash size (e.g., “4MB”). Users can also set options to erase the entire flash before writing, compress data during transfer, or reset the device after flashing.

⚙️ Key details

Unlike the Python-based esptool, esptool-js does not implement generation of binary images out of ELF files and does not include companion tools similar to espefuse.py and espsecure.py.

Handling Flash Images

  • Merged .bin files: These are contiguous images where bytes between partitions are 0xFF. Using writeFlash erases every sector from the start of the image through its end, which also erases NVS and factory partitions within that span.
  • Sparse Intel HEX files: These leave gaps out. The parseIntelHex function splits the file into one { data, address } entry per contiguous region. If two regions share a 4 KiB flash sector, parseIntelHex throws an error. To ensure only covered sectors are erased, users should keep eraseAll: false and compress: true.

🚀 Availability

Developers can integrate esptool-js into web applications using the following endpoints:

  • Use https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/bundle.js for a single-file browser load. Dependencies such as pako are inlined, so no import map is required.
  • Use https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/lib/index.js for Node and bundlers. An API documentation reference is available for detailed class and method information.

Puppeteer, a JavaScript library for controlling Chrome or Firefox, has updated its installation behavior to accommodate modern package manager security defaults, while expanding its capabilities with new API support and an MCP server integration.

🔍 Overview

Puppeteer provides a high-level API to control Chrome or Firefox over the DevTools Protocol or WebDriver BiDi. Modern package managers, including npm, pnpm, Yarn, Bun, and Deno, now block dependency install scripts by default. Because Puppeteer traditionally downloaded a compatible Chrome binary during the npm i puppeteer installation step, this security feature can prevent the browser from downloading, leading to runtime errors.

To address this, developers have two main options:

  • Manually download the required browsers after installation by running the command npx puppeteer browsers install.
  • Configure the package manager to allow the specific install script to run. For example, with npm, developers can add “puppeteer” to the “allowScripts” array in the package.json file.

Alternatively, developers can use npm i puppeteer-core to install Puppeteer as a library without automatically downloading Chrome.

🧩 How it works

A standard workflow involves launching a browser instance, opening a new page, navigating to a URL, and interacting with elements using locators and keyboard actions. The library supports querying elements by CSS selectors or by accessible names, allowing for robust interaction with web content.

item.title: Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes
item.description:
Weaviate Helm Chart v17.1.0: Raft Bootstrap and Resource Limit Changes

The Weaviate Helm chart has released version 17.1.0, introducing significant updates to cluster bootstrapping in Weaviate v1.25 and removing default resource constraints to improve module performance.

🔍 Overview

Weaviate can be deployed to a Kubernetes cluster using the provided Helm chart, provided that Helm is installed. Version 17.1.0 of the chart addresses specific infrastructure changes required by newer Weaviate releases and resolves performance restrictions in default configurations.

⚙️ Key Details: Cluster Bootstrapping

Weaviate v1.25 introduced a significant change in how the cluster bootstraps, driven by the adoption of a Raft-based consensus model.

  • The podManagementPolicy was changed from OrderedReady to Parallel.
  • This change is required for the Raft cluster to bootstrap properly, as all pods must start simultaneously.
  • Once the Raft cluster is established, rolling updates are possible.
  • This change takes effect when migrating from versions prior to v1.25 or when bootstrapping a new v1.25 cluster.

⚠️ Migration Steps

When upgrading from a version older than v1.25 to v1.25 or above, the following one-time operation is required:

  1. Delete Weaviate’s Statefulset.
  2. Update the Statefulset settings to reflect the new policy.

This process will not remove your data but is necessary to make the update of Statefulset settings possible.

📉 Key Details: Resource Limits

In Weaviate-Helm version 17.1.0, the default resource limits and requests defined in the values.yml file have been removed.

  • Reason: Previous default values restricted the performance of some modules, making them almost unusable unless resources.requests and resources.limits were overridden.
  • Impact: Modules deployed with default values prior to version 17.1.0 will have their resource values removed upon upgrading to 17.1.0 or above, resulting in no constraints on memory or CPU usage.
  • Recommendation: To prevent modules from consuming all system resources, users are strongly recommended to override modules.$MODULE.resources.requests and modules.$MODULE.resources.limits with values that suit their specific system.

🛠 Release Process

To release a new version of the chart, the following steps are taken:

  • Bump the chart version in ./weaviate/Chart.yaml.
  • Create a commit and an annotated tag matching the version number (prefixed with v, e.g., v1.4.3).
  • Push the commit and tag to the repository.
  • A GitHub Action creates a drafted release with the packaged chart attached.
  • The draft is edited to include release notes and published.

item.title: New TypeScript AMQP 0-9-1 Client Supports Browsers and Node.js
item.description:
New TypeScript AMQP 0-9-1 Client Supports Browsers and Node.js

A new TypeScript client for AMQP 0-9-1 has been released, supporting both Node.js and browsers via WebSocket. Developed and supported by CloudAMQP, the library is designed to replace other Node.js AMQP libraries and enables developers to write browser applications that communicate directly with AMQP servers.

🔍 Overview

The library is Promise-based, integrating well with async/await, and works with any AMQP 0-9-1 broker, including RabbitMQ, LavinMQ, and Apache Qpid. It supports self-hosted instances and managed providers such as CloudAMQP or Amazon MQ, as they all use the same protocol. The codebase is transpiled from TypeScript, and running Node with the --enable-source-maps flag ensures proper stack traces.

🧩 How it works

The library offers two levels of abstraction:

  • High-level (AMQPSession): Provides automatic reconnection and consumer recovery. Users utilize queue() and exchange() handles for reconnect-safe operations.
  • Low-level (AMQPClient / AMQPWebSocketClient): Offers direct channel access with methods such as queueDeclare, basicPublish, and basicConsume.

The transport mechanism is determined by the URL scheme: amqp:// or amqps:// utilizes TCP, while ws:// or wss:// uses WebSocket. To establish a session with automatic reconnection and consumer recovery, developers call AMQPSession.connect(url, options).

⚙️ Key details

The library is secure by default; publishes are not fulfilled until data is sent on the wire or, if Publish Confirms are enabled on the channel, until the server acknowledges that the message has been enqueued.

Message Acknowledgement

  • Messages are acknowledged after the callback returns.
  • If the callback throws, the message is negatively acknowledged (nacked) and requeued.
  • Developers can override this behavior by calling msg.ack() or msg.nack() directly.
  • Subscriptions created via queue.subscribe() are automatically re-established after a reconnection.
  • The sub.consumerTag and sub.channel properties reflect the current consumer and are updated upon reconnection.
  • Prefetch parameters in subscribe settings can be used to configure Quality of Service (QoS) on each connection.

Codec Registry Developers can opt into a codec registry to handle serialization and deserialization based on content-type and content-encoding:

  • Built-in parsers support JSON and text; built-in coders support gzip and deflate.
  • Defaults can be set to avoid repeating configurations on every publish.
  • When codecs are configured, msg.body contains the decoded value; otherwise, it is a Uint8Array. The CodecMode generic infers this type at compile time.
  • Specific publishes can override defaults by passing contentType or contentEncoding in the options.
  • Custom codecs can be registered by merging them with the built-ins.
  • Decode failures surface as a plain Error rather than an AMQPError; in subscribe() contexts, these failures nack the message, honoring requeueOnNack.

item.description:
AI coding toolkit updates remove legacy DSH support and refine agent rules

The professional-grade AI coding toolkit has released an update that removes support for the legacy DeepSeek Harness (DSH) code and refines how agent instructions are managed across multiple platforms. This update introduces machine-enforced safety features, expands skill libraries, and adjusts how global and local installations interact with project-specific rules.

🔍 Overview

The toolkit now includes 116 skills and 44 agents, offering multi-platform support for tools such as Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Gemini, Cline, Roo Code, Aider, Augment, Antigravity, Codex CLI, and opencode. It features machine-enforced safety, lifecycle hooks, persona presets, opt-in plugin packs, and benchmark tooling. The update explicitly removes the last DeepSeek Harness (DSH) code (v5.4.0). Consequently, ai-toolkit dsh is now an unknown command, --editors dsh is an unknown editor, and the toolkit no longer migrates old DSH project skills or registry entries.

🧩 How it works

  • Security Auditing: The security-auditor reviews source code, configurations, and dependencies, then verifies fixes with local checks.
  • Agent Instructions: Project instructions reside in a committed AGENTS.md file, which CLAUDE.md imports. The ai-toolkit adopt-agents-md command moves existing CLAUDE.md content to AGENTS.md. This process ensures that nothing truncates the file, with Codex project_doc_max_bytes raised and 24,000-byte Antigravity warnings accounted for.
  • Rule Management: A toolkit-generated AGENTS.md file (marked # AI Toolkit Instructions) is no longer imported, preventing Claude from loading rules from ~/.claude/rules/ twice. The adopt-agents-md command refuses to merge into this specific file. Agents other than Claude Code do not read that file.
  • Hooks and Triggers: Hooks run from the hooks.json directory and gate only run_command. Workspace rules carry trigger frontmatter and are designed to fit Antigravity’s size limits.
  • MCP Server Integration: Injected servers, such as rag-mcp, are written to each claude-switch profile, similar to mcp install. The remove-mcp and uninstall commands clean these entries. Registered rules that require an MCP server only reach a file when its readers have that server; rag-mcp-legal-rules remains an opt-in feature.
  • Local vs. Global Installation: install --local installs everything a client can load from $HOME before project files, using the recorded global profile. The --no-global flag opts out of this, and update preserves the profile.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model Support: Skills and defaults reference Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, while the Codex reference includes GPT-6.1 Sol.
  • Language Scoping: Language knowledge skills (e.g., rust-rules, kotlin-patterns) are scoped to languages used by registered projects. After running ai-toolkit install --local in at least one project, the global install turns off other languages’ skills through skillOverrides in ~/.claude/settings.json to prevent their descriptions from loading into every session.
  • Workflow Migration: All 13 legacy workflows remain available alongside their skills. The Doctor tool checks the global global_workflows directory and provides migration instructions for specific clients.
  • Status Reporting: Redirecting account status to a legacy-encoded pipe preserves readable progress bars and paths. A refused usage read displays Unavailable: rate_limited, retry in 40m from the provider’s Retry-After header (retry_after_seconds in JSON), occurring once per account.
  • Requirements: The toolkit requires Node.js >= 18 and Python >= 3.11. It will not run on /usr/bin/python3 if it is Python 3.9.

💡 Why it matters

Claude Code automatically picks up the 116 skills, 44 agents, quality hooks, and the safety constitution. Global Claude MCP installs reach every claude-switch profile. This structure ensures that developers can maintain rigorous security standards and efficient agent behavior across a wide range of coding environments without manually managing redundant rule files or unsupported legacy commands.

SMART SDK and AgentCore Simplify WhatsApp Agent Deployment on AWS

Across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications, but building a robust agent on top of it requires handling complex, type-dependent payloads, media processing pipelines, and strict compliance rules. To simplify this process, SMART (Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit) is available as an open source Python SDK and Terraform stack that provides the full channel layer for agents running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

🧩 How it works

SMART allows you to provide an agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and it handles the underlying channel logic. The architecture utilizes the following services:

  • AWS End User Messaging Social: Receives inbound WhatsApp messages and routes them to the processing layer.
  • AWS Lambda: Handles the channel logic, including verifying SNS message signatures, normalizing payloads, and rate-limiting users (20 messages per minute by default).
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Provides the runtime, memory, and observability for the agent.
  • Supporting Services: Amazon DynamoDB (optional, for per-user state), AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon CloudWatch, and Amazon S3 supply state management, credentials, monitoring, and storage.

The AgentCore runtime hosts and scales the agent without requiring infrastructure management. AgentCore memory persists conversation history across sessions and deployments, scoped automatically to each phone number. The create_session_manager() function binds the agent to this memory, with a default retention period of 7 days. Frameworks such as Strands Agents get memory wired automatically, while LangGraph and Pydantic-AI can integrate with the conversation loop.

⚙️ Key details

Wiring up a custom WhatsApp agent typically involves configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning specific system behaviors. SMART abstracts these complexities, including:

  • Inbound message authentication and normalization.
  • Processing pipelines for media such as voice notes, images, and documents.
  • Durable schedules for reminders and authenticated paths for external systems to trigger outbound messages.
  • Compliance with Meta’s requirement that messages sent more than 24 hours after the user’s last message must use pre-approved templates.
  • Handling of intermediate tool outputs (like button lists or progress updates) to prevent conversation history corruption.

🚀 Availability

SMART is an open source solution. A single command deploys the entire infrastructure to your AWS account. Webmotors, originally scoped as a two-month engagement, compressed delivery to six weeks and moved their internal team into controlled production ahead of a full launch using this approach.

Env Variable Description

  • Listens on PORT (default 8080) and serves MCP at /mcp, with a health check at /health.
  • --http and JEV_BROWSER_TRANSPORT=http are equivalent; containers and service units can select the transport without argv.
  • It speaks MCP 2026-07-28 and falls back to stateless serving for 2025‑era clients, keeping no sessions so any number of replicas can sit behind a plain load balancer.
  • Each in‑flight call runs its own headless Chromium for up to its time budget (max_seconds, default 180, cap 600). Admitted requests are capped at JEV_BROWSER_MAX_CONCURRENCY (default 4; excess gets 429).
  • Reverse proxy or load balancer read timeouts must be at least as long as the largest max_seconds you allow, or it will cut healthy runs short.
  • The server itself speaks plain HTTP; terminate TLS at a reverse proxy or load balancer before exposing it beyond loopback, and put connection limits and request rate limits at that ingress.

item.title: Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly
item.description:
Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly

Datasette Lite allows the full server-side Datasette Python web application to run directly inside a user’s browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide.

🧩 How it works

When the demo is launched, the browser downloads and executes a full Python interpreter, installs the datasette package and its dependencies, and starts the application in a Web Worker.

  • Datasette pages are displayed in a full-window <iframe> pointing to URLs under /app/<session>/.
  • A service worker (sw.js) intercepts requests (link clicks, form submissions, fetch calls, static assets) and relays them to the Datasette ASGI application running in Pyodide.
  • This architecture supports Datasette’s own JavaScript, plugin assets, POST forms, CSRF protection, sign-in cookies, and file uploads/downloads.
  • Streaming responses, such as server-sent events or CSV exports, are processed as they are produced.
  • If a client disconnects or aborts a fetch, the Datasette application is notified that the client has disconnected.
  • Cookies are stored in a cookie jar inside the Python ASGI bridge, lasting until the tab is closed or reloaded.

⚙️ Key details

  • Browser Requirements: Requires a browser with service worker support. Private browsing modes that disable service workers are not compatible.
  • Web Worker Support: Requires module workers (Chrome 80, Safari 15, Firefox 114 or later).
  • Python Version: Uses Python 3.14 from Pyodide 314.0.8.
  • Error Handling:
    • 503 returned if the tab has already been closed or reloaded.
    • 504 returned if the tab stops answering partway through a request (after four minutes).
    • 500 returned if the Pyodide worker itself fails.
    • 409 returned if a tab was opened before an incompatible update.
  • Session Management: Each tab receives a random session identifier, allowing multiple instances with different data to run simultaneously.
  • Navigation: The page mirrors the iframe’s location into its fragment to ensure the back button works and URLs are bookmarkable.
  • Security: Links to external sites open in a new window with noopener.

🚀 Availability and Versioning

Datasette Lite uses the most recent Datasette release from PyPI by default, including alpha and beta previews.

  • Stable Release: Append ?ref=stable to the URL.
  • Specific Release: Pass a version number as ?ref=.
  • Preview Release: ?ref=pre is equivalent to leaving ?ref out.
  • Source Code: Other ?ref values are treated as branches, tags, or commits in the simonw/datasette GitHub repository.
    • Example: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=main runs the latest development code.
    • Short SHAs made up only of digits are read as version numbers; full 40-character SHAs are required for specific commits.
    • ?ref values that look like version numbers are always installed from PyPI.
  • Plugin Installation: ?install= works for plugins, requiring a commit with a pyproject.toml.
  • CORS Handling: GitHub source zip files are downloaded through a Cloudflare Worker to add necessary CORS headers.

item.title: Langfuse SDKs migrate to OpenTelemetry in latest releases
item.description:
Langfuse SDKs migrate to OpenTelemetry in latest releases

Langfuse has released new versions of its Python and JavaScript/TypeScript SDKs, both rewritten to be built on OpenTelemetry (OTel). The legacy SDK clients are deprecated, and developers are advised to adopt the new instrumentation methods and use the Observations API v2 for querying traces.

🧩 How it Works

The new SDKs use OpenTelemetry to handle observability and tracing. For real-time data ingestion, the only supported path is OpenTelemetry, combined with the Observations API v2 and Metrics API v2.

  • Python: Use the langfuse package with get_client(), start_as_current_observation, or the @observe decorator. Spans are created using context managers and are automatically closed when exiting their blocks.
  • JavaScript/TypeScript: Use the @langfuse/tracing package with startActiveObservation or startObservation, along with LangfuseSpanProcessor from the @langfuse/otel package.

For offline evaluation, regression testing, and prompt management, both SDKs provide dedicated packages (langfuse for Python and @langfuse/client for JavaScript).

⚙️ Key Details

The legacy v2 and v3 client APIs are deprecated. Querying traces using legacy endpoints like GET /api/public/traces or api.traceList is no longer recommended; developers must use GET /api/public/v2/observations.

  • Data Freshness: All GET APIs other than the OpenTelemetry ingestion path can be up to 10 minutes behind.
  • Python Installation: Install via pip install langfuse.
  • JavaScript Installation: Install via npm install @langfuse/tracing @langfuse/otel "@opentelemetry/sdk-node@<0.300".
  • Version Requirements: The JS/TS SDK v6 requires Langfuse Cloud or self-hosted Langfuse v4.59.0 or later. OpenTelemetry JS SDK 2.x is supported; 3.x is not supported yet.

🚀 Availability

The new SDKs are available as the latest releases for both platforms, with JavaScript targeting Node.js 22+ for core tracing and OTEL helpers.

  • CLI Management: Users can review and change the approved app list from the terminal on macOS without opening the Codex app. Listing apps is free, but allowing or revoking requires the user to be at the machine.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Open-Weight Models Support Explicit Prompt Caching
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Open-Weight Models Support Explicit Prompt Caching

Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. This update allows developers to reuse computed prompt prefixes across requests, reducing input costs and response latency by reading repeated context from cache instead of processing it again.

🔍 Overview

Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix. When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from the cache and processes only the remainder. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, meaning savings grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input, but Amazon Bedrock manages the cache automatically.

🧩 How it works

Developers can use implicit caching, which works automatically on a best-effort basis, or explicit caching, where specific reusable prefixes are marked.

  • Implicit Caching: Amazon Bedrock reuses eligible prefixes automatically. In a conversation, each request resends the full context, so the previous request becomes the cached prefix for the next one. As recommended by the prompt caching guide, static content should be placed first and dynamic content last to keep the start of the prompt stable. If an early part changes, the cache is rebuilt from that point.
  • Explicit Caching: Users mark the end of each reusable prefix with a cache breakpoint. Content up to each breakpoint is written to cache once and read on later requests, while content after the last breakpoint is processed on every request. Users can add several breakpoints, up to the model’s maximum, to cache layers that change at different rates. This method limits cache writes to the shared prefix, preventing higher write-rate billing for content that is never read back on models that charge for cache writes.

On the Chat Completions API, explicit caching is configured using prompt_cache_options with the mode set to explicit, plus one or more prompt_cache_breakpoint markers.

⚙️ Key details

Feature Detail
Caching Modes Implicit (automatic) and Explicit (user-marked)
Data Privacy Prompts and outputs are not shared with the model provider or used to train models
Configuration Use prompt_cache_breakpoint markers on the Chat Completions API
TTL Time to live resets with each cache hit; specific durations vary by model
Minimums Minimum token count and maximum breakpoints vary by model; check the model card

Amazon Bedrock checks the prompt cache for a matching prefix, reads a matching prefix from cache, and writes new cacheable content to cache.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Model availability and prompt caching support vary by AWS Region. An AWS account with access to the selected model on Amazon Bedrock is required. Developers should check the model card for the Regions that the model supports, as well as specific caching modes, minimum prefix lengths, and entry retention times.

Requests are sent to the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your selected Region, authenticated with a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key.

item.title: Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates
item.description:
Nucleoid adds terminal workspace, bare-word syntax, and comment updates

Nucleoid has updated its developer experience and language syntax with a new full-screen terminal workspace, support for bare-word assignments, and changes to how comments and conditional logic are handled.

🔍 Overview

Nucleoid is a next-generation logic programming language built on structured objects and their relationships, extending the traditional Knowledge Graph. It uses a minimum-token syntax for logic representation and a declarative execution model, eliminating the need for LLMs to manually manage control flow, state propagation, and other imperative constructs.

🧩 How it works

The new interactive interface offers a top-level tab layout, with two tabs reserved for future views. A multiline editor sits at the bottom, featuring autocomplete for keywords, built-ins, and model properties, plus in-session input and result history. Results can be inspected in Text, JSON, or Table formats without re-running the program; arrays of objects render as table rows, while other JSON values display in property/value or index/value views.

Key input behaviors include:

  • Enter inserts a newline.
  • F5 runs the entire editor content.
  • Ctrl-J inserts an automatically indented newline.
  • Tab accepts autocomplete or indents.
  • Ctrl-Space opens suggestions.
  • Ctrl-P / Ctrl-N recalls input while preserving an unfinished draft.
  • F1-F3 switch tabs, F6 changes the result view, and Ctrl-Up / Ctrl-Down select earlier results.
  • Mouse clicks select tabs, views, and results; click/drag edits the cursor/selection, and the wheel scrolls individual panes.
  • Ctrl-C cancels input, Ctrl-Q exits, and .help lists all controls.

⚙️ Key details

  • Assignment Syntax: Assignments can be written as target is value. Quotes are optional around a single word. For example, a is 5 and o.x is "good" are valid. If the value is a bare word that does not match a defined variable, class, function, or built-in, it stores its own text.
  • Conditional Branches: In conditionals like a is A if c else B, a bare word in a branch is read as a variable, class, function, or built-in if it exists; otherwise, it reads as its own text. Parenthesized operands are not treated as words, so a is (A if c else B) requires A and B to be defined.
  • List and Dictionary Items: Inside is values, list items, dictionary values, or named arguments can also be bare words.
  • Comments: Hash (#), double-slash (//), and non-nesting block comments (/* ... */) all work in files and interactive interfaces. Comments take delimiter priority outside literals, meaning // is a comment, not an empty regex (use /(?:)/ for an empty-matching regex). Comments retain newlines and source positions and cannot join tokens or supply indentation. Unclosed block comments report SyntaxError: Unterminated block comment at its opening slash.
  • Plain Mode: Running nucleoid --plain provides a line-oriented interface. Piped stdin or redirected stdout automatically selects this mode. Body lines are prefilled with indentation after the .. prompt, and blank lines submit the block.

🚀 Availability

Install the CLI from crates.io using the command: cargo install nucleoid. The standard nucleoid command opens the full-screen terminal workspace from any directory. File execution and the --json and --graph flags retain their existing behavior. References NUC 76, NUC 93, and NUC 94 document the removal of the --c-style-comments, --is-assignment, and --conditional-words flags, respectively.

Component Role

  • Users sign in with an IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS CLI, call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly, then point Codex to the approved model and run a safe task.
  • The direct runtime call isolates AWS access problems and creates a short‑lived AWS session that validates model invocation in the selected Region.
  • Settings are kept in user‑level or managed configuration so a repository cannot change the provider.

⚙️ Key details

  • Quick‑start options include Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, ADOT, and Amazon CloudWatch setup.

    • Grant only the Bedrock model inference permissions needed by Codex plus any validation commands and the selected observability destination.
    • Prepare a non‑production repository and designate a rollback owner.
    • Add each pilot user to a dedicated group in the workforce identity system and provision that group to IAM Identity Center.

🚀 Availability

  • The model identifier used by Codex is the Codex model ID.
  • The AWS profile selects the IAM Identity Center session; the Region setting tells Codex which AWS Region to use.

💡 Why it matters

  • Managed gateway options (AgentCore Gateway) simplify routing and security controls without custom infrastructure.

item.title: OpenHands Cloud Introduces Scheduled and Event-Driven Automation Execution Service
item.description:
OpenHands Cloud Introduces Scheduled and Event-Driven Automation Execution Service

A new automation execution service has been developed for OpenHands Cloud, providing support for both scheduled and event-driven automation workflows.

🔍 Overview

The Automation Service allows users to manage and execute agent workflows based on predefined schedules or external triggers. Key features include:

  • Scheduled Automations: Run OpenHands conversations on a cron schedule.
  • Event-Driven Automations: Trigger automations via webhooks, such as GitHub events.
  • API Key Management: Per-user API keys for secure automation access.
  • Run History: Track automation runs with status and results.

🧩 How it works

System responsibilities are divided across several components:

  • Automation Service: Owns automation definitions, cron scheduling, webhooks, run history, dispatch, and sandbox lifecycle orchestration.
  • Agent Server and OpenHands/software-agent-sdk: Execute agent conversations and own agent/tool behavior, workspaces, events, and API endpoints.
  • OpenHands/typescript-client: Provides typed browser access to the Agent Server API.
  • OpenHands/OpenHands: Owns the Agent Canvas UI and frontend integration.

The codebase is structured into specific modules:

File Description
app.py FastAPI application entry point
router.py API routes for CRUD operations
scheduler.py Background scheduler for cron jobs
dispatcher.py Dispatches pending runs to OpenHands
models.py SQLAlchemy models
schemas.py Pydantic schemas for API

⚙️ Key details

The service is built using Python 3.12+ and uses uv for dependency management. For storage, it utilizes PostgreSQL, with testcontainers available for testing.

Database migration and creation rules include:

  • SQLite databases are migrated on startup.
  • PostgreSQL databases are not migrated on startup unless AUTOMATION_RUN_MIGRATIONS_ON_STARTUP=true (or 1) is set. When set, each replica runs alembic upgrade head before serving requests, using an advisory lock so concurrent replicas take turns. A failed migration stops the replica from starting.
  • Setting AUTOMATION_CREATE_DATABASE_IF_MISSING=true (or 1) instructs migrations to connect to the postgres database and create the target database if missing. This requires the database user to have the CREATEDB privilege.

🚀 Deployment

For local development, dependencies can be installed using uv sync --group dev, and the application can be run with uv run uvicorn openhands.automation.app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload.

Container deployment can be built and run using Docker:

  • docker build -t automation -f containers/Dockerfile .
  • docker run -p 8000:8000 automation

The service is deployed via the deploy repository at https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/deploy. Docker images are automatically built and pushed to ghcr.io/openhands/automation on every push to main and on tags.
